Executive Summary

This report presents the findings of an automated GDPR compliance analysis covering 1000 websites across multiple categories and regions. The analysis examines pre-consent tracking behavior, dark pattern usage in cookie consent banners, and the effectiveness of various privacy-enhancing technologies (PETs) as countermeasures.

A large majority of sites (87.5%) were found to set tracking cookies before any user consent was given, violating GDPR Article 5(3). The average compliance score across all sites was 27.4 out of 100.

A large majority of sites (89.7%) employed at least one dark pattern in their cookie consent interface, undermining the principle of freely given consent.

Among the browser-based PETs evaluated, brave_shields proved most effective, reducing tracker exposure by an average of 22.8%.

Reject Actually Reduces Trackers

Of the 595 sites that displayed a consent banner, only 160 (26.9%) provided a visible "Reject All" button. 24.9% of sites offered equal click effort for accept and reject.

Clicking "Reject All" reduced tracker counts on only 7.6% of sites and eliminated all trackers on just 12.2%. On average, sites retained 6.9 trackers after rejection compared to 6.6 before interaction.

Accept vs. Reject Click Effort

Accepting consent required an average of 1 click(s), while rejecting required 1.3 click(s) — 148 sites (24.9%) offered equal effort for both actions. 435 sites (73.1%) had no visible reject button at all.

User Recommendations

  1. Install brave_shields for the strongest browser-level tracker blocking (avg. 22.8% reduction).
  2. privacy_badger is a good alternative with 21.0% avg reduction.
  3. When a site uses Didomi, the reject/decline mechanism is most effective (PET score: 24.9).
  4. Be cautious with Usercentrics-powered banners — they scored lowest as a privacy tool (PET score: 9.1).
  5. For maximum protection, combine brave_shields with a site using Didomi (est. 42.0% effective).
  6. Always click 'Reject All' when possible — some CMPs actually honour it.
  7. Differential privacy with a moderate epsilon can protect individual browsing data when publishing aggregate compliance statistics.

Methodology

This analysis was conducted using an automated pipeline built in Python. Websites were crawled using Playwright in three consent states: no interaction, accept all, and reject all. Cookies and HTTP requests were captured in each state.

Sites analyzed: 1000  |  Categories: 12  |  Regions: 54

Pipeline Components

  1. Crawler — Playwright-based browser automation capturing cookies, HTTP requests, consent banners, and screenshots.
  2. Classifier — Cookie/tracker classification using EasyList, EasyPrivacy, Disconnect lists, and a fallback heuristic.
  3. Dark Pattern Detector — Detects 7 types of deceptive consent UI patterns.
  4. Compliance Scorer — GDPR compliance scoring (0–100) based on 6 weighted criteria.
  5. Metrics Engine — Aggregate statistics across all sites.
  6. PET Evaluator — Tests 7 browser-level PET configurations.
  7. DP Reporter — Applies differential privacy to aggregate metrics.
  8. CMP Analyzer — Evaluates consent management platforms as privacy tools.
  9. Visualizer — Generates 11 publication-quality figures (300 DPI).

Limitations

  • Consent banner interaction relies on keyword-based button detection; some non-standard banners may be missed.
  • Analysis is based on a single crawl per site; dynamic content may vary across visits.
  • Browser PET evaluation with extensions requires manual extension installation.
  • Results may vary depending on geographic location and VPN configuration.
